exam.subject: Agriculture
exam.title: ESSCE 2020 – Agriculture

parts.title: Part I – Multiple Choice Questions
parts.instructions: Part I contains 80 questions; each carries 1 point. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the answer sheet with a pencil.

parts.title: Part II – Short Answer/Essay Questions
parts.instructions: Part II contains seven short answer/essay questions (20 points). Answer all of them on the separate answer sheet.

source.note: Scanned paper (20 pages, no figures); OCR text checked against the page images (garbled items such as Q17, Q36, Q64 and Q75 were read from the images).

exam.answer_key_note: No official key exists. All answers were solved independently and checked against the Eritrean MoE Agriculture textbooks Grades 11 and 12 (extracted text with page markers). See confidence and review_flag on each question.

questions.stem: The process of joining two plants to allow them to grow as a single unit is referred to as
explanation_steps: Grafted fruit trees are made of two parts joined together: the rootstock (lower part, root system) and the scion (upper part, shoot), which heal and grow as one plant (textbook Figure 3.29, 'A grafted plant').

Grafting uses a scion with two or more buds; budding (including T-budding) is a special case that uses only a single bud. Layering roots a stem while it is still attached to the parent plant, and transplanting moves seedlings, so neither joins two plants. The general term is grafting. Answer: B.
tips: Budding = one bud; grafting = scion with 2 or more buds. Both join a scion to a rootstock, but the general term in the question is grafting.

similar_questions.stem: In a grafted fruit tree, the lower part that forms the root system is called the
explanation_steps: Textbook: the lower section of the tree is the rootstock (root system) and the upper section is the scion (shoot).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A farming system, where communities are settled in permanent villages, cultivate crops and keep livestock is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Sedentary agro-pastoralism: this is a system where communities are settled in permanent villages, cultivate crops, and keep livestock. This system is also called mixed farming.'
Transhumance, semi-nomadism and pastoralism all involve moving with livestock, and intensive commercial farming is a specialised system. Answer: B.
tips: Sedentary agro-pastoralism = mixed farming (67 % of the population, moist and arid highlands).

similar_questions.stem: The seasonal movement of people and their livestock between lowland and highland grazing areas, returning to a home base, is called
explanation_steps: Semi-nomadic pastoralists move seasonally with their herds and return to a permanent base; this seasonal movement is transhumance.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Farming Systems in Eritrea – c) Sedentary agro-pastoralism

questions.stem: All of the following have positive impact on the environment, except
explanation_steps: Textbook 1.2.8: 'Deforestation, over-cultivation, overgrazing, soil contamination and air pollution' are negative effects of agriculture; 'afforestation, land reclamation, the appropriate use of animal manure as fertilizer and the pollination activities of bees are positive effects.'
Over-cultivation exhausts soil nutrients and exposes the soil to erosion. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a positive effect of agriculture on the environment?
explanation_steps: Textbook lists the pollination activities of bees among the positive effects.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Identify the dominant farming system in Eritrea.
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.1: nomadic pastoralism 11 %, semi-nomadic pastoralism 22 %, sedentary agro-pastoralism 67 % of the population.
Sedentary agro-pastoralism (mixed farming) is by far the largest. Answer: C.
tips: Remember 11 – 22 – 67 (nomadic – semi-nomadic – sedentary).

similar_questions.stem: According to the textbook, about what percentage of Eritrea's population practises semi-nomadic pastoralism?
explanation_steps: Table 1.1: semi-nomadic pastoralism 22 %.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about nomadic pastoralism?

options.A: It is dominant in the semi desert agro ecological zones.
options.B: In this system, it is difficult for the government to provide social services.
options.C: It is the least dominant among the farming systems in the country.
options.D: It is practiced in the moist and arid highlands of Eritrea.

explanation_steps: Textbook: nomadic pastoralism is prevalent in the semi-desert agro-ecological zones (Red Sea coastal areas and north-western Eritrea); it is difficult for government to provide education and health services; it involves only 11 % of the population (the smallest share).
It is sedentary agro-pastoralism, not nomadism, that exists in the moist and arid highlands. So D is false. Answer: D.
tips: Highlands → settled mixed farming; semi-desert → nomads; spate areas such as Sheeb → semi-nomads.

similar_questions.stem: Where in Eritrea is semi-nomadic pastoralism typically practised?

options.B: Spate irrigation areas such as Sheeb

explanation_steps: Textbook: semi-nomadic pastoralism occurs in the spate irrigation areas such as the Sheeb area in the Northern Red Sea Zone.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.3 Farming Systems in Eritrea – a) Nomadic pastoralism

questions.stem: Among the following, choose the one which is not a poultry disease.
explanation_steps: Textbook (commercial poultry): 'Diseases such as New Castle disease, Gumboro, Marek's disease and respiratory diseases are common in poultry production.'
Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis) is described in Grade 12 as a bacterial disease of livestock (grazing animals) and humans, not a poultry disease. Answer: B.
tips: Poultry diseases to remember: Newcastle, Gumboro, Marek's, respiratory diseases.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following diseases is caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis?
explanation_steps: Textbook: anthrax is a bacterial disease of animals and humans caused by Bacillus anthracis.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: In plant production, the end products of photosynthesis are
explanation_steps: Textbook Figure 3.4: CO₂ + H₂O + sunlight → sugar + O₂. Light energy is stored as chemical energy in sugar.
Carbon dioxide is a raw material, not a product; proteins and fatty acids are made later from the sugars. Answer: B.
tips: Raw materials: CO₂ and water; products: sugar and O₂.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a raw material of photosynthesis?
explanation_steps: CO₂ + H₂O + light → sugar + O₂; CO₂ is taken in from the air.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The study of soils from the point view of plants is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'edaphology is the study of the soil from the point of view of plants. It deals with soil properties in relation to plant production.'
Pedology examines the soil's origin, classification and description. Answer: B.
tips: Edaphology → plants; Pedology → origin, classification, description.

similar_questions.stem: A soil scientist who describes and classifies soils by their origin is working in
explanation_steps: Textbook: pedology examines the soil's origin, classification and description.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.1 Soil Formation – approaches to the study of soil

questions.stem: Which of the following agricultural constraints is classified as a yield defining factor?
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.3: yield-defining factors are CO₂ concentration, solar radiation, temperature, humidity, crop physiology, altitude and latitude, animal species, livestock breeds, crop types and varieties.
Nutrients and feed (nutrition) are yield-limiting factors; pests and diseases are yield-reducing factors. Answer: B.
tips: Defining = given (climate, genetics); Limiting = water and nutrients/feeding; Reducing = pests, diseases, weeds, pollutants.

similar_questions.stem: Weeds in a crop field are classified as a
explanation_steps: Table 1.3: pests, diseases, weeds, pollutants and stress are yield-reducing factors.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The dry matter components of animal feeds contain all of the following, except
explanation_steps: Textbook: six nutrients are recognised – water, carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals. 'The five nutrients (carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins and minerals) are collectively known as dry matter (DM).'
Dry matter is what remains after the water is removed. Answer: D.
tips: DM = feed − water. Organic matter = DM − minerals.

similar_questions.stem: A farmer gives a cow 10 kg of fresh grass containing 70 % water. How much dry matter does the cow receive?
explanation_steps: Dry matter = 100 % − 70 % = 30 % of the feed.
0.30 × 10 kg = 3 kg. Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 1.2.1 Feeds and Feed Composition – nutrients and dry matter

questions.stem: The male, in the castes of the colony of bees is the
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Three types of individual exist in a colony of bees: the queen (a fertile female), workers (infertile females) and drones (males).'
Answer: C.
tips: Drones only mate with virgin queens, have no sting and die after mating.

similar_questions.stem: In a honeybee colony, the individuals that build the hive, collect nectar and defend the colony are the
explanation_steps: Textbook: workers build and repair the hive, search for nectar and pollen, produce wax and honey, feed the young and protect the hive.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a function of soil?

options.A: It is a habitat of soil organisms.
options.B: It is a medium for plant growth.
options.C: It is a system of water supply and purification.
options.D: It is a medium for engineering workers.

explanation_steps: Textbook (Figure 2.2): the five major ecological roles of soil are medium for plant growth, habitat for soil organisms, recycling of nutrients and wastes, water supply and purification, and engineering medium (foundation and building material).
A to D are all soil functions ('engineering workers' is a misprint of 'engineering works'), so none of them is a non-function. Answer: E.
tips: Five roles: plants, organisms, recycling, water, engineering.

similar_questions.stem: Using soil as a foundation for roads and buildings is an example of soil acting as
explanation_steps: Textbook: soil is an engineering medium (foundation and building material).
Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Option D reads 'a medium for engineering workers' – a misprint of 'engineering works/medium'. Read as intended, all four statements are soil functions, so E is keyed.

questions.stem: As wind direction is to wind vane, atmospheric pressure is to the
explanation_steps: A wind vane shows wind direction; the instrument that measures atmospheric pressure is the barometer (textbook list of meteorological equipment: rain gauges, anemometers, barometers, evaporation pans, max–min thermometers).
An anemometer measures wind speed, an evaporation tank/pan measures evaporation, a radiometer measures radiation and a thermo-hydrograph records temperature and humidity. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: As rainfall is to rain gauge, wind speed is to the
explanation_steps: The anemometer measures wind speed.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about the effects of salinity on plant growth?

options.A: It brings ionic imbalance in the plant.
options.C: It can have direct toxicity effect.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'There are three main effects of salinity on plants: direct toxicity (e.g. from sodium, chloride, boron); ionic imbalance in the plant; reduction in water availability by lowering the osmotic potential' (physiological drought).
All four statements are true, so none is untrue. Answer: E.
tips: Salinity causes 'physiological drought': plants suffer lack of water even though the soil contains enough water.

similar_questions.stem: Why can plants on saline soils wilt even when the soil is moist?

options.A: The salts lower the osmotic potential of the soil solution, so water is less available

explanation_steps: Textbook: salinity reduces water availability by lowering the osmotic potential – physiological drought.
Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – c) Salinity and its effects on plant growth

questions.stem: Plants which develop flower nodes in less than 12 hours of daylight are called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Short-day plants: these are plants which develop (flowering, node formation, tuberization etc.) with less than 12 hours of daylight.'
Long-day plants need more than 12 hours; day-neutral plants are unaffected by day length. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Plants that flower over a wide range of day lengths are
explanation_steps: Textbook: day-neutral plants are unaffected by photoperiod.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.7 Climatic Factors – b) Classification based on day length

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a wildlife animal?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Wildlife includes all non-domesticated plants, animals and other organisms.'

Table 2.7 (major vertebrate wildlife of Eritrea) lists the greater spotted eagle (birds), monkey (primates), jackal (carnivores) and snakes (Serpentes, reptiles). All four are wild animals. Answer: E.
tips: If none of the options is a domesticated animal, 'None of the above' is correct.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT wildlife?
explanation_steps: Wildlife = non-domesticated organisms; the dairy cow is a domestic animal.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: A growing crop that is ploughed under to enrich soil is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Green manure crops or cover crops are plants sown to enrich the soil when ploughed or tilled under the soil later.' Green-manure crops (e.g. clovers, alfalfa, vetches) are ploughed in while green.
Humus is decomposed organic matter; compost is decomposed plant and animal waste made in a heap; crop rotation is a cropping system. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which crops are best used as green manure because they add nitrogen to the soil?

options.B: Legumes such as vetch, clover and cowpea

explanation_steps: Textbook: green-manure crops such as clovers, alfalfa, soybeans, vetches and cowpeas provide nitrogen when ploughed under green.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.12 Biological Properties – decomposition, humus and green manure

additional_textbook_refs.section: 3.2.2 The Classification of Field Crops – green-manure crops

questions.stem: Decomposition process is affected by
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Decomposition rates are fastest when the soil provides optimal growth conditions for the micro-organisms. These include: soil temperatures near 20 °C; moisture of 50 to 70 per cent of the soil's water-holding capacity; aeration – oxygen must be in adequate supply; a food supply or fresh organic matter additions.'
All four are listed. Answer: E.
tips: Decomposers need warmth (~20 °C), moisture (50–70 % of water-holding capacity), oxygen and food (organic matter).

similar_questions.stem: Decomposition of organic matter is fastest at soil temperatures near
explanation_steps: Textbook: optimal conditions include soil temperatures near 20 °C.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.12 Biological Properties – c) Decomposition processes and nutrient cycling

questions.stem: One of the following is not agriculture-based industry.
explanation_steps: Textbook 1.2.4: 'Agriculture is the basis of the development of agriculture-based industries such as the food-processing, textile, leather, brewery and sugar industries. Edible oil is extracted from sesame, cottonseed and Niger seed.'
Metallurgy processes metal ores (minerals), not farm products. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which crop supplies raw material to the brewery industry in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Malting barley is used for the manufacture of beer.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not true about rhizosphere?

options.A: Rhizosphere has a low PH compared to the environment.
options.B: Rhizosphere has lower O₂ concentration compared to the environment.
options.C: Rhizosphere environment has lower CO₂ concentration compared to the environment.
options.D: Rhizosphere has larger number of microorganisms compared to the environment.
options.E: Rhizosphere has more microbial activity compared to the environment.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'When compared to the atmosphere, the rhizosphere environment has a lower pH, lower O₂ concentration, higher CO₂ concentration, larger numbers of microorganisms, and more microbial activity.'
Roots and microbes respire, using O₂ and releasing CO₂, so CO₂ is HIGHER, not lower. Answer: C.
tips: Respiration in the root zone: O₂ goes down, CO₂ goes up, pH goes down (CO₂ forms carbonic acid).

similar_questions.stem: The rhizosphere is best described as

options.A: the zone of intense microbial activity around plant roots
options.B: the layer of dead leaves on the soil surface
options.C: the parent rock under the soil
options.D: the air above a crop canopy

explanation_steps: Textbook: the rhizosphere is an intense zone of stimulated microbial activity around the root.
Answer: A.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.12 Biological Properties – plant roots and the rhizosphere

questions.stem: All of the following are greenhouse gases, except
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The main greenhouse gases are carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and nitrous oxide (N₂O).'
Nitrogen gas (N₂), the main gas of the air, is not a greenhouse gas. Do not confuse N₂ with N₂O. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which greenhouse gas is released mainly by ruminant livestock and flooded rice fields?
explanation_steps: Methane (CH₄) is produced by microbial fermentation in the rumen and in waterlogged soils.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The name given for the conservation of genetic resources in gene banks is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Ex-situ means conserving genetic resource in gene banks. In-situ refers to conserving genetic resources on farmers' fields and in enclosure areas.'
Answer: C.
tips: Ex = outside the natural place (gene bank); in = in the natural place.

similar_questions.stem: Conserving local crop varieties by encouraging farmers to keep growing them in their fields is
explanation_steps: Textbook: in-situ conservation is on farmers' fields and in enclosures.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is incorrect about soil colour?

options.B: Whitish soils indicate existence of salt accumulation.
options.D: Dark colours indicate accumulation of organic matter.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Black and dark colours indicate accumulation of organic matter. Grey colours show iron DEPLETION. Reddish-brown colours indicate well-drained soils. Whitish soils are related to the various salts found in arid and semi-arid regions.'
Statement A says accumulation instead of depletion, so it is incorrect. Answer: A.
tips: Grey = waterlogged, iron reduced and removed (depleted); red/brown = oxidised iron, good drainage.

similar_questions.stem: A reddish-brown subsoil colour usually indicates that the soil is
explanation_steps: Textbook: reddish-brown colours indicate well-drained soils.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.10 Other Physical Properties of Soil – soil colour

questions.stem: Soils that predominate in arid and semi-arid regions are
explanation_steps: Textbook: alkaline soils (pH often 9–10 when Na₂CO₃ is present) 'predominate in arid and semi-arid regions, where the annual rainfall is insufficient to meet evapotranspiration rates.'
Low rainfall does not leach the bases (Ca, Mg, Na), so they accumulate and raise the pH. Answer: D.
tips: High rainfall → leaching → acidic soils; low rainfall → bases accumulate → alkaline soils.

similar_questions.stem: Heavy rainfall over many years tends to make soils
explanation_steps: Leaching removes basic cations and leaves acidic ones, lowering pH.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – b) Soil reaction

questions.stem: Soil colloid is derived from a Greek word which means
explanation_steps: Textbook: '"Soil colloid" is derived from a Greek word, meaning "glue-like". Colloids could be organic or inorganic matter.'
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Soil colloids can be
explanation_steps: Textbook: colloids could be organic or inorganic matter (humus and clay).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.2.11 Chemical Properties of Soil – a) Soil colloid

questions.stem: The type of germination, in which the cotyledons emerge above the soil surface, is known as
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Hypogeal germination occurs when the cotyledon does not emerge above the soil surface. Epigeal germination takes place when the cotyledon emerges above the soil surface.'
Answer: B.
tips: Epi = above; hypo = below.

similar_questions.stem: In maize, the cotyledon stays below the soil surface during germination. This is
explanation_steps: Cotyledon remaining below the soil = hypogeal germination.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: Quick-growing annuals that are sown in the field where crops have failed to produce grain are known as
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Catch crops or emergence crops: these are quick-growing annuals that are sown in the field where crops have failed to produce grain. Short-season crops such as millet are often used.'
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Crops that are cut and fed green (fresh) to livestock are called
explanation_steps: Textbook: soiling crops are cut and fed green to animals.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The largest river basin in Eritrea, in terms of area coverage is
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 2.12 (area of watershed): Red Sea 44,690 km²; Barka-Anseba 39,510 km²; Mereb-Gash 23,200 km² (16,730 km² within Eritrea); Danakil Depression 10,530 km²; Setit 4,045 km².
The Red Sea basin is the largest. Answer: E.
tips: Order by area: Red Sea > Barka-Anseba > Mereb-Gash > Danakil > Setit (smallest area, but the only perennial river with the largest runoff).

similar_questions.stem: Which Eritrean river basin has the largest estimated runoff even though its area is the smallest?
explanation_steps: Table 2.12: Setit 4,045 km² but runoff 5,800–8,000 million m³ (it rises in the rainy central Ethiopian highlands).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.4.3 The Major River Basins of Eritrea (Table 2.12)

questions.stem: One of the following is different from the rest.
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Most cereal crops such as barley, maize and wheat are monocots. Dicots have two cotyledons. This group includes crops such as beans and peas'; 'Tomato, beans and pumpkin are examples of dicot plants.'
Barley is the only monocot (and the only cereal) in the list. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a monocot crop?
explanation_steps: Cereals such as sorghum, maize, barley and wheat are monocots.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.1 Crops – a) Morphological description of plants

questions.stem: Plants requiring medium supply of water are called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'xerophytes (desert plants) endure great water loss without injury; mesophytes are those that require medium supplies of water; hydrophytes are those plants growing best with abundant water e.g. rice.'
Hydroponics is soil-less growing, and saprophytes feed on dead matter. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Rice, which grows best with abundant water, is classified as a
explanation_steps: Textbook example: hydrophytes such as rice.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.1.6 Water – plant types by water requirement

questions.stem: The branch of horticulture which deals with vegetables is
explanation_steps: Textbook branches of horticulture: pomology – fruit crops; olericulture – vegetables (e.g. lettuce, cabbage); floriculture – flowers and house plants; ornamental and landscape horticulture.
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Growing roses and other cut flowers for sale belongs to
explanation_steps: Floriculture deals with flowers and house plants.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Of the following horticultural production systems, the dominant one in Eritrea is
explanation_steps: Textbook 3.5.2: horticultural production systems are open-field (under natural soil and climatic conditions), protected (glasshouses, poly-tunnels, plastic covers) and hydroponics (without soil).

Protected production and hydroponics need expensive structures and inputs and exist only on a few commercial farms; almost all Eritrean vegetables and fruits (home gardens and irrigated farms) are grown in open fields. Answer: B.
tips: 'Controlled' production is another name for protected production.

similar_questions.stem: A horticultural system in which temperature, light and humidity are regulated inside glasshouses is
explanation_steps: Textbook: protected production takes place in glasshouses, poly-tunnels and under plastic covers where climatic factors are controlled.
Answer: B.

textbook_ref.note: The textbook describes the three systems but does not state in words which is dominant in Eritrea.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: which system is dominant in Eritrea is not stated; B (open field) is keyed from the textbook descriptions and general knowledge.

questions.stem: A method of disease control, that involves the use of natural enemies such as predators and pathogens, is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Biological control: involves the use of natural enemies such as predators and diseases for the control of pests.'
IPM combines several methods; mechanical control uses hand-picking, traps, etc.; chemical control uses pesticides. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Combining resistant varieties, cultural practices, natural enemies and careful pesticide use to manage pests is called
explanation_steps: Using several compatible control methods together is integrated pest management (IPM).
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 3.3.6 Weeds, Insects and Diseases – methods of pest control

questions.stem: Growing of two or more crops simultaneously in the same field in the same season is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Inter-cropping is one form of mixed cropping where two or more crops are grown on the same land and year in a particular row arrangement.'
Relay cropping sows the second crop before the first is harvested (partial overlap); crop rotation grows crops one after another; mulching and contouring are not cropping systems. Answer: C.
tips: Same time, same field → mixed/intercropping. One after the other → rotation/sequential.

similar_questions.stem: Growing different crops one after the other on the same piece of land in successive seasons is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: in crop rotation, crops are grown in sequence one after the other on the same land.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: A product-product relationship where an increase or decrease in the level of one product does not affect the production level of the other product is known as
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Supplementary products exist when an increase or decrease in the level of one product does not affect the production level of the other product. An example is the production of maize and poultry.'
Competitive products compete for resources; joint products are produced together (wheat and straw); complementary – one increases the other; antagonistic – one harms the other. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Growing maize after a bean crop increases maize yield because beans fix nitrogen. Beans and maize are then
explanation_steps: Textbook: complementary products – an increase in one product increases the other (bean–maize example).
Answer: C.

questions.stem: In plant sciences, grading refers to the

options.A: covering of soil surface with organic or inorganic materials.
options.C: practice of discarding poor quality seedlings and keep only the good ones in nursery.
options.D: transfer of seedlings from the seedbeds, seed trays, or boxes to containers and a nursery.
options.E: processes of joining two plants to allow them grow as a single unit.

explanation_steps: Textbook (nursery practices): 'It is good practice to discard the poor quality seedlings and keep only the good ones. This practice is known as grading.' About 10–20 % poor seedlings is acceptable.
A = mulching, B = pruning, D = transplanting (pricking out), E = grafting. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Moving young seedlings from a seedbed into individual pots or containers is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: transplanting is the transfer of seedlings from seedbeds, trays or boxes to containers.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Among the following, the leading milk breed in the world is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The Holstein-Friesian breed is the leading breed in the world for milk production.'
Hereford, Angus, Shorthorn and Galloway are beef breeds. Answer: D.
tips: Dairy: Holstein-Friesian, Jersey, Guernsey, Brown Swiss, Ayrshire. Beef: Angus, Hereford, Charolais, Simmental, Brahman.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a beef cattle breed?
explanation_steps: Hereford is listed among beef breeds.
Answer: C.

additional_textbook_refs.section: 1.3 Routine Management Practices – beef and dairy breeds

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a cattle breed in Eritrea?
explanation_steps: Textbook: cattle breeds of Eritrea are Barka, Arado and Arebo (Dewhin near the Sudan border).
Hassani (Shukria) is a GOAT breed, known for its milk and frequent twins and triplets. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an Eritrean goat breed?
explanation_steps: Textbook goat breeds: Hassani (Shukria), Sudanese Desert (Barka or Tsa'adi), Worre and Afar. (Rashaidi is a sheep type.)
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.section: 2.3 Biodiversity – agro-biodiversity (breeds of cattle and goats)

questions.stem: Among the following protected areas, select the one established mainly for Nubian ibex?
explanation_steps: Textbook list of protected areas: Gash-Setit (elephants), Semenawi-Bahri (remnant forests and habitats), Buri Peninsula (wild ass), Yob and Nakfa in northern Eritrea (Nubian ibex).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: The Buri Peninsula protected area was established mainly for the
explanation_steps: Textbook: Buri Peninsula – wild ass.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: The removal of seedlings, which are grown too closely in order to give an optimum space and nutrient for the remaining plants is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Thinning involves the removal of some plants so that the remaining plants are able to get enough space and nutrients for good growth.' Seeds in a nursery are sown at high density.
Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which nursery practice balances the shoot and root system of seedlings by cutting?
explanation_steps: Textbook: pruning balances the length of the shoot and the root system of seedlings.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: All of the following are agronomic practices, except
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.2 (on cropland): agronomic practices = use of fertilizer, cover crops, crop rotation, intercropping, tillage practices, grass strips along the contour, agroforestry. 3.3.4 adds crop-residue and organic-matter management (mulching).
Stone bunds are listed under PHYSICAL conservation measures (terraces, stone bunds, diversion ditches, waterways, gully control). Answer: D.
tips: Physical = structures built from stone/soil (terraces, bunds, check-dams); agronomic = how the crop and soil are managed.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a physical soil and water conservation measure?
explanation_steps: Table 3.2: terraces are physical conservation measures.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Lines drawn on a map connecting points of equal elevation are called
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Contour: a line joining points on the same elevation either on the ground or on a map.'
Horizontal interval = horizontal distance between two points; vertical interval = difference in height; isotherms join equal temperature; isobars join equal pressure. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: On a map, lines joining places with equal mean temperature are called
explanation_steps: Isotherms join places of equal temperature.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements is false about agronomic soil and water conservation practices?

options.A: They are mainly cultural practices which conserve soil and water.
options.C: They include use of organic and inorganic fertilizers.
options.D: They are usually linked with annual crops.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Agronomic practices are those cultural or biological practices for management of annual and perennial crops that promote SWC. These practices include the use of organic manure and inorganic fertilizers, cover crops, crop rotation, inter-cropping…'
They are repeated every season with the crop (temporary), unlike physical structures such as terraces and stone bunds, which are permanent. So B is false. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT an agronomic SWC practice?
explanation_steps: Check-dams are physical structures (gully control); the rest manage crops and soil.
Answer: C.

textbook_ref.note: Definition and list verified; the textbook does not use the word 'temporary/permanent' for agronomic practices.

questions.stem: Among the components of land degradation, the one that is synonymous with organic matter decline is
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Biological degradation is usually synonymous with a decline in organic matter, yet it also applies when there is a decline in beneficial soil fauna.'
Acidification is chemical degradation; compaction is physical degradation. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Salinization and nutrient depletion are examples of
explanation_steps: Textbook: chemical degradation includes nutrient loss, salinity and acidification.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: The detachment of small soil particles by raindrops is known as
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.1: 'Splash erosion is the detachment and airborne movement of small soil particles caused by the impact of raindrops on soil.'
Sheet erosion also involves removal down slope by thin flowing water; rills and gullies are channels. Answer: D.
tips: Order of water erosion: splash → sheet → rill → gully.

similar_questions.stem: Removal of a thin, fairly uniform layer of soil over a whole slope by runoff water is
explanation_steps: Sheet erosion removes soil evenly downslope in a thin layer.
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A type of irrigation system, where water is applied to a level area surrounded by earth bunds, is called

similar_questions.stem: Diverting seasonal flood flows from the highlands onto lowland fields is
explanation_steps: Textbook: spate irrigation involves the diversion of spate (flood) flows.
Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a fixed resource?
explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The level of some resources, such as buildings, machinery and implements, is fixed over a planning period, irrespective of the rate of production. These are known as fixed resources. Resources like fertilizers, seeds, etc., whose use varies with the rate of production, are known as variable resources.'

questions.stem: The purpose of pruning trees is to

options.A: develop a strong structure to hold fruits.
options.C: keep the trees within the desired shape.

explanation_steps: Textbook: fruit trees require formative pruning (training) to develop a good framework, and pruning balances the shoot and root systems of seedlings.
Pruning also removes dead, diseased and crowded branches (health), keeps trees at a manageable size and shape, and stimulates vigorous new growth. All four purposes are correct. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Pruning a young fruit tree in the nursery to build a good framework of branches is called
explanation_steps: Textbook: fruit trees require formative pruning or training for developing a good framework.
Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Textbook gap: only 'developing a good framework' (A) is stated in the textbook; E (all of the above) is keyed from standard horticultural knowledge.

questions.stem: The largest and smallest agro-ecological zones of Eritrea are __ and __, respectively.

questions.stem: Wildlife decline in a given environment could be caused by

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed in the textbook as a cause of wildlife decline?

questions.stem: Which of the following is false about production function?

options.A: It describes the relationship between input and output.
options.B: Production function can be expressed in tabular, graphic and algebraic forms.
options.C: In production function, the output is dependent upon the input(s).
options.D: Production function is a linear graph between input and output.
options.E: In a single variable production function, only one variable is allowed to vary.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'The relationship between inputs and outputs can be described as a production function … output is dependent upon input(s). Production functions can be expressed in three forms: tabular, graphic and algebraic.'
The fertilizer-response curve in the textbook rises, levels off and falls (diminishing returns), so a production function is generally NOT a straight line. Answer: D.
tips: Law of diminishing returns → the total product curve bends; it is not linear.

similar_questions.stem: In the production function Y = f(X), Y represents
explanation_steps: Output (Y) depends on input (X).
Answer: B.

questions.stem: A farmer bought a tractor for 600,000.00 Nakfa. If the salvage value of the tractor is 25,000.00 and the life time of the tractor is 10 years, what will be the book value of the tractor, in Nakfa, at the end of year 5?
explanation_steps: Textbook Equation 4.11 (straight line): annual depreciation = (CP − SV) ÷ E = (600,000 − 25,000) ÷ 10 = 57,500 Nakfa.
Accumulated depreciation after 5 years = 5 × 57,500 = 287,500 Nakfa.
Book value = cost − accumulated depreciation = 600,000 − 287,500 = 312,500 Nakfa. Answer: D.
tips: Traps: 57,500 (E) is one year's depreciation; 287,500 (C) is the accumulated depreciation, not the book value.

similar_questions.stem: A water pump costs 90,000 Nakfa, has a salvage value of 10,000 Nakfa and a life of 8 years. Its book value after 3 years is
explanation_steps: Annual depreciation = (90,000 − 10,000) ÷ 8 = 10,000 Nakfa.
Book value = 90,000 − 3 × 10,000 = 60,000 Nakfa. Answer: A.

questions.stem:
Based on their carbon source, bacteria can be divided into two large groups, name them. (2 points)

questions.answer:
1.1 Autotrophic bacteria – obtain their carbon by fixing atmospheric CO₂.
1.2 Heterotrophic bacteria – require (organic) carbon compounds as a food source; they are important in decomposing organic matter.

subparts.question: Group 2
steps: Use organic carbon compounds as food.

They are important in decomposing organic matter.'

questions.stem:
a) What is Brucellosis? (1 point)
b) How can Brucellosis be controlled? (2 points)
questions.answer:
a) Brucellosis is a contagious bacterial disease (caused by Brucella species – B. abortus, B. melitensis, B. ovis, B. suis) of domestic animals and humans (zoonosis; called undulant fever in humans). It mainly affects the reproductive organs and causes abortion (5–8 months of pregnancy in cows), joint inflammation and endometritis.
b) Control: (1) proper hygiene and the use of appropriate vaccines; (2) burn or bury contaminated material, aborted foetuses and foetal membranes, and clean and disinfect the premises; (3) destroy (test and slaughter) infected animals; (4) take hygienic precautions when handling abortions and avoid drinking unpasteurised milk or milk products from infected herds.

subparts.label: a
subparts.question: What is Brucellosis?
subparts.answer: A bacterial (Brucella) disease of domestic animals and humans (undulant fever) that attacks the reproductive organs and causes abortion.

subparts.label: b
subparts.question: How can Brucellosis be controlled?
subparts.answer: Hygiene and vaccination; burn/bury aborted foetuses and membranes and disinfect premises; destroy infected animals; avoid unpasteurised milk and handle abortions hygienically.

explanation_steps: Textbook: 'Brucellosis is a bacterial disease of domestic animals and humans … In humans, brucellosis is known as undulant fever.' It affects the uterus, testis, accessory sex glands, lymph glands and joints and causes abortion.

Textbook control: 'Brucellosis can be controlled by proper hygiene and the use of appropriate vaccines. Contaminated material, aborted fetuses and fetal membranes should be burned or buried, and premises cleaned and disinfected. Infected animals should be destroyed … the drinking of unpasteurised milk or milk products should be avoided.'
a) 1 point: bacterial (Brucella) disease of animals and humans that causes abortion. b) 0.5 point for each of four control measures.
marking_points: a) 1: bacterial disease caused by Brucella, affecting animals and humans (undulant fever), causing abortion/infertility.

b) 0.5 each (max 2): hygiene; vaccination; burning/burying aborted foetuses and membranes + disinfecting premises; destroying/test-and-slaughter of infected animals; avoiding unpasteurised milk/care when handling abortions.
tips: Brucellosis = 'contagious abortion'; always mention it is zoonotic (humans get it from raw milk and aborted material).

similar_questions.stem: How is tuberculosis spread to humans and how can it be controlled in a herd?
similar_questions.answer: Mainly by drinking raw milk and eating undercooked meat from infected animals (and by breathing in the bacteria). Control: proper hygiene and sanitation, avoiding overcrowding, and testing and isolating infected animals (pasteurise milk).
explanation_steps: Textbook: TB is controlled by hygiene, sanitation, avoiding overcrowding and testing and isolating infected animals.

textbook_ref.section: 1.5.1 Common Diseases and Parasites – a) Bacterial diseases (brucellosis)

questions.stem:
Mixed farming systems have both advantages and disadvantage. List down three disadvantages of mixed farming. (3 points)
3.1 ______
3.2 ______
3.3 ______
questions.answer:
Any three of (textbook Table 1.2):
• Free grazing results in overgrazing, which causes land degradation.
• High labour input is required.
• It is expensive for first-time farmers (high starting capital).
• In some cases, specialization in certain commodities offers more profit than diversification.
• It requires high technical know-how to run both crop cultivation and animal husbandry.
• It is practised only in areas where both crop and livestock production are possible; crop cultivation is difficult in marginal and arid areas with low and sporadic rainfall.

subparts.question: Disadvantage 1
subparts.answer: Free grazing causes overgrazing and land degradation.

subparts.question: Disadvantage 3
subparts.answer: Expensive for first-time farmers / requires high technical know-how.

explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.2 lists six disadvantages of mixed farming systems (see the answer).
1 point for each correct disadvantage (maximum 3).
marking_points: 1 each (max 3): overgrazing/land degradation from free grazing; high labour input; expensive for first-time farmers; specialization may be more profitable; needs high technical know-how in both crops and livestock; only possible where both crops and livestock can be produced (not in marginal/arid areas).
tips: Don't give advantages by mistake (manure for crops, residues for feed, draught power, insurance against drought).

similar_questions.stem: List three advantages of mixed farming.
similar_questions.answer: Any three: crops feed livestock and livestock give manure; diversified produce and balanced food; animal traction (oxen, camels, donkeys) for ploughing; continuous cash income; insurance during drought; better use of land and labour; crop residues used as feed.
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 1.2 advantages.

questions.stem:
Name three major areas where forest biodiversity is concentrated in Eritrea. (3 points)
4.1 ______
4.2 ______
4.3 ______
questions.answer:
4.1 The Eastern Escarpment (e.g. Semenawi Bahri / Green Belt).
4.2 The riverine forests of the Western Lowlands (along the Gash, Barka, Setit and Anseba rivers).
4.3 Limited pockets of forest in the Northern Highlands.

subparts.question: Area 2
subparts.answer: Riverine forests of the Western Lowlands

subparts.question: Area 3
subparts.answer: Pockets of forest in the Northern Highlands

explanation_steps: Textbook 2.3.1 a): 'In Eritrea, forest biodiversity is concentrated in three areas: the Eastern Escarpment, the riverine forests of the Western Lowlands, limited pockets of the forests of the Northern Highlands.'
1 point for each area.
marking_points: 1 each: Eastern Escarpment; riverine forests of the Western Lowlands; pockets of forest in the Northern Highlands.
tips: Mangroves on the Red Sea coast are also forests, but the textbook's three areas are the ones asked.

similar_questions.stem: Which two tree species dominate the remnant forests of the sub-humid Eastern Escarpment?
similar_questions.answer: Juniperus procera (tsihdi) and Olea africana (wild olive, awlie).
explanation_steps: Textbook: the dominant forest types of the sub-humid escarpment include Juniperus procera and Olea africana.

questions.stem:
Write down any three criteria used in the selection of a nursery site. (3 points)
5.1 ______
5.2 ______
5.3 ______
questions.answer:
Any three of:
• Climate – the site should suit the requirements of the plants and be protected from wind.
• Land gradient – the land should be level (gentle, well drained).
• Water supply – access to clean water, free of salts.
• Soil – the land for a field nursery should be fertile.
• Access – easy road access (to bring inputs and distribute seedlings).

subparts.question: Criterion 1
subparts.answer: Reliable supply of clean, salt-free water.

subparts.question: Criterion 3
subparts.answer: Easy road access and a suitable climate protected from wind.

explanation_steps: Textbook 3.5.4: 'The criteria used in selecting a site for a nursery are: climate …; land gradient …; water supply …; soil …; access …'
1 point for each criterion with a short explanation (maximum 3).
marking_points: 1 each (max 3): suitable climate/protection from wind; level land; clean salt-free water supply; fertile soil; easy road access.
tips: Remember 'CLAWS': Climate, Level land, Access, Water, Soil.

similar_questions.stem: Name the three types of nursery described in the textbook.
similar_questions.answer: Peasant nursery (farmers raise their own seedlings), standard nursery (commercial seedling production) and intermediate or temporary nursery (seedlings kept temporarily before distribution).
explanation_steps: Textbook 3.5.3.

questions.stem: Summarise briefly the major morphological differences between monocotyledonous and dicotyledonous crops. (3 points)
questions.answer:
Monocots vs dicots (textbook Table 3.1):
1. Embryo with a single cotyledon vs two cotyledons.
2. Pollen with a single furrow or pore vs three furrows or pores.
3. Flower parts in multiples of three vs multiples of four or five.
4. Major leaf veins parallel vs reticulate (net-veined).
5. Stem vascular bundles scattered vs arranged in a ring.
6. Roots adventitious (fibrous) vs developing from the radicle (tap root).
(Seeds cannot be split into two equal halves vs can be split into two halves.) Examples: monocots – barley, maize, wheat, sorghum; dicots – beans, peas, tomato, pumpkin.
explanation_steps: Textbook Table 3.1 gives seven major morphological differences.
0.5 point for each correct pair of contrasting features (maximum 3 points = six differences).
marking_points: 0.5 each (max 3): cotyledons one vs two; pollen one pore vs three; flower parts 3s vs 4s/5s; leaf veins parallel vs reticulate; vascular bundles scattered vs ring; roots adventitious vs from radicle (tap); seed not divisible vs divisible into two halves.
tips: Write the answer as a two-column table: feature | monocot | dicot.

similar_questions.stem: Give two examples each of monocot and dicot crops.
similar_questions.answer: Monocots: barley, maize (also wheat, sorghum). Dicots: beans, tomato (also peas, pumpkin).
explanation_steps: Textbook examples.

questions.stem:
A soil in the field has a total volume of 1 m³. Out of the total volume, 3/5 is solid and the rest is pore space. The weight of the solid part of the soil is 1.4 Mg.
7.1 Calculate the particle density of the soil sample? (1.5 points)
7.2 What is the bulk density of the soil sample? (1.5 points)
questions.answer:
7.1 Volume of solids Vs = 3/5 × 1 m³ = 0.6 m³. Particle density = mass of dry solids ÷ volume of solids = 1.4 Mg ÷ 0.6 m³ ≈ 2.33 Mg/m³ (= 2.33 g/cm³).
7.2 Bulk density = mass of dry solids ÷ total volume = 1.4 Mg ÷ 1 m³ = 1.4 Mg/m³ (= 1.4 g/cm³).
(Check: porosity = 1 − BD/PD = 1 − 1.4/2.33 = 0.40 = 2/5 of the volume, as given.)

subparts.question: Calculate the particle density of the soil sample.
What is the bulk density of the soil sample?

explanation_steps: Textbook worked example: bulk density = weight of oven-dry soil ÷ total volume (solids + pores); solid particle density = weight of oven-dry soil ÷ volume of solids only.
7.1: Vs = 0.6 m³ → PD = 1.4 ÷ 0.6 = 2.33 Mg/m³ (1 formula/Vs, 0.5 answer with unit).
7.2: Vt = 1 m³ → BD = 1.4 ÷ 1 = 1.4 Mg/m³ (1 formula, 0.5 answer with unit).
Particle density is always larger than bulk density because the pores are excluded from the volume.
marking_points: 7.1 (1.5): Vs = 0.6 m³ (0.5); PD = mass/volume of solids (0.5); = 2.33 Mg/m³ with unit (0.5).
7.2 (1.5): BD = mass/total volume (0.5); substitution 1.4/1 (0.5); = 1.4 Mg/m³ with unit (0.5).
tips: Same mass on top in both formulas; only the volume changes: solids only (PD) or total (BD).
1 Mg/m³ = 1 g/cm³.

similar_questions.stem: A 1 m³ block of soil contains 0.55 m³ of solids with a dry mass of 1.43 Mg. Find its particle density, bulk density and porosity.
explanation_steps: PD uses the volume of solids; BD uses total volume; porosity = pore volume ÷ total volume.
